Maximum likelihood estimation of \(\theta\) and \(m\) based on Etienne sampling formula

Source: R/etienne.R
optim_etienne.Rd

Etienne sampling formula is an exact solution of Hubbell's (2001) model where a single deme is connected to a single regional pool with dispersal limitation. In Hubbell's (2001) model, a dead individual is immediately replaced by offspring of other local individuals or by immigrants from the regional pool with probability \(m\). The diversity of the regional pool is described by \(\theta\). Etienne sampling formula infers \(m\) and \(\theta\) based on one sample of the deme. If there is no dispersal limitation, the sample can be considered as representative of the regional pool, corresponding to the limiting case \(m=1\), where the Etienne sampling formula becomes equivalent to the Ewens sampling formula.

optim_etienne() computes the maximum likelihood estimates of the fundamental biodiversity number \(\theta\) and the immigration rate \(m\) of Etienne's sampling formula (Etienne 2005) for a species abundance distribution \((n_1, ..., n_k)\) sampled from a single local community that receives immigrants from a neutral metacommunity. The input should be a vector and initial values of \((\theta, m)\) can be supplied with the argument init_vals = c(theta_init, m_init) with the condition theta_init > 0 and 0 < m_init < 1.

The coefficients \(K(D,A)\) are computed once with logkda(). The log-likelihood is then maximised with the box-constrained quasi-Newton method L-BFGS-B (stats::optim()) using the exact gradient, on the scale \((\log\theta, \log I)\) with \(I=\frac{m}{1-m}(J-1)\). The optimisation is The likelihood surface can be multimodal, with narrow peaks next to ridges that run to the edge of the search domain, so it is first profiled in both directions: on a grid of 61 values of \(\log I\) the likelihood is maximised over \(\theta\), and on a grid of 61 values of \(\log\theta\) it is maximised over \(I\). The optimisation is then run from every local maximum of the two profiles, from init_vals, and from the Ewens estimate with \(m\) close to 1, and the best result is kept.

Usage

optim_etienne(
  input_abundances,
  init_vals = c(10, 0.5),
  lower = c(1e-06, 1e-08),
  upper = NULL,
  ci = FALSE,
  level = 0.95
)

Arguments

input_abundances

a vector of integers (species abundances); species with zero abundance are ignored

init_vals

initial values of (theta, m), a vector of two real numbers

lower, upper

bounds of the search interval for c(theta, m)

ci

if TRUE, also return likelihood-ratio confidence intervals (default FALSE)

level

confidence level of the intervals (default 0.95)

Value

A list with

theta

fundamental biodiversity number \(\theta\), a real value

m

immigration rate, a real value

I

rescaled immigration rate, \(I=\frac{m}{1-m}(J-1)\), a real value

logl

maximal log-likelihood, a real value; it is comparable with the logl value of optim_ewens() and optim_pitman()

converged

TRUE if the optimiser reported convergence, or stopped on a line-search failure at a point where the (projected) gradient vanishes

se_theta, se_m, se_I

standard errors of theta, m and I, real values

local_maxima

a data frame of the distinct local maxima, best first, with columns theta, m, I, logl and boundary

ci_theta, ci_m, ci_I

only if ci = TRUE: confidence intervals, vectors c(lower, upper)

Search interval and boundary warnings

By default \(\theta\) is searched in [1e-6, 100 J] and \(m\) in [1e-8, 1 - 1e-8], where J is the number of individuals. A warning is issued if an estimate lies on the edge of its interval; use lower and upper to change it. An estimate of \(m\) at its upper bound means that the data show no evidence of dispersal limitation: the Ewens model (optim_ewens()) is then adequate.

Uncertainty

The standard errors se_theta, se_m and se_I are obtained from the inverse of the Hessian of the log-likelihood (on the scale \((\log\theta, \log I)\), then the delta method). They account for the correlation between the two parameters, unlike the Std_ columns of the TeTame software, and are NA when an estimate lies on a bound of the search interval. As the likelihood is often strongly asymmetric, the likelihood-ratio confidence intervals returned with ci = TRUE are preferable: for each parameter, the range over which the profile log-likelihood (maximised over the other parameter) stays within qchisq(level, 1) / 2 of its maximum. A limit equal to a bound of the search interval means that the interval extends at least to that bound. When the likelihood runs along a ridge towards \(m = 1\), \(\theta\) and \(m\) are weakly identified, the chi-squared approximation is conservative, and the intervals are wider than their nominal level (in 200 simulations with \(\theta = 20\), \(m = 0.1\), \(J = 1000\), 95% intervals covered the true values in 99.5% of the replicates). When the likelihood runs along a ridge towards \(m = 1\), the Ewens sampling formula should be used.

Local maxima

local_maxima lists the distinct local maxima of the likelihood found by the optimisation (TeTame reports a second maximum in the same way). The first row is the global maximum. Points on a bound of the search interval are flagged (boundary); they are kept only when they are local maxima of the profile likelihood there. Two flagged points with the same likelihood typically mark the two ends of a flat ridge, along which the data cannot discriminate between \(\theta\) and \(m\).

Log-likelihood

logl is on the same scale as the logl of optim_ewens() and optim_pitman() (see logl_etienne()). The Ewens model is the Etienne model with \(m = 1\), so the two models are nested and can be compared by the likelihood-ratio statistic \(2(\mathrm{logl}_{Etienne} - \mathrm{logl}_{Ewens})\) or by AIC.

Sample size

The computing time of \(K(D,A)\) grows roughly as \(J^2\): about 2 s for \(10^4\) individuals and 30 s for \(4 \times 10^4\) on a typical computer. Unlike the other estimators of the package, the Etienne model is therefore practical up to about \(10^5\) individuals. Please exercise caution for large datasets. One practical recommendation for large datasets is to consider them as a collection of demes and to use the multi-deme model instead of the Hubbell model.

References

Etienne, R. S. (2005) A new sampling formula for neutral biodiversity. Ecology Letters 8: 253-260.

See also

logl_etienne(), logkda(), optim_ewens(), optim_multideme()

Examples

## Example of Etienne (2005), supplementary material: theta = 7.05, m = 0.226
zoo <- c(8, 5, 3, 2, 1, 1)
et <- optim_etienne(zoo)
et
#> $theta
#> [1] 7.047969
#> 
#> $m
#> [1] 0.2263591
#> 
#> $I
#> [1] 5.559197
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -28.56215
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $se_theta
#> [1] 15.10683
#> 
#> $se_m
#> [1] 0.3349456
#> 
#> $se_I
#> [1] 10.63283
#> 
#> $local_maxima
#>      theta         m        I      logl boundary
#> 1 7.047969 0.2263591 5.559197 -28.56215    FALSE
#> 

## Is there evidence of dispersal limitation?
## Compare with the nested Ewens model
ew <- optim_ewens(zoo)
2 * (et$logl - ew$logl) # likelihood-ratio statistic
#> [1] 0.3577858

## Confidence intervals; a sample with two local maxima (TeTame test data)
optim_etienne(zoo, ci = TRUE)[c("ci_theta", "ci_m")]
#> $ci_theta
#>       lower       upper 
#>    0.811495 2000.000000 
#> 
#> $ci_m
#>      lower      upper 
#> 0.04102535 0.99999999 
#> 
optim_etienne(c(15, 81, 80, 2, 1, 2))$local_maxima
#>       theta           m          I      logl boundary
#> 1 21.747365 0.006867291    1.24466 -195.2637    FALSE
#> 2  1.056303 0.980993441 9290.41505 -195.2851    FALSE
